In children aged 12 years or above, the Asthma Control Test (ACT) scores below 20 had a low sensitivity but high specificity for predicting exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB) [4,2]. Specifically, in the older children, ACT scores below 20 had a sensitivity of 32.3% and a specificity of 90.3% as a predictor of EIB [4,2]. This suggests that while the ACT is not very good at ruling out EIB, it can be useful for confirming EIB in older children when scores are low.

To differentiate children with difficult-to-treat asthma from those with severe asthma that is resistant to traditional therapies, a multidisciplinary systematic assessment is essential [1, 2, 4, 5]. This includes evaluating comorbid conditions such as nasal disease, eczema, food allergy, and obesity, as well as assessing treatment-related issues like adherence to therapy and inhaler technique [1, 4, 5]. Identifying modifiable factors, such as dysfunctional breathing and environmental exposures, and non-modifiable factors, such as the presence of asthma-mimicking conditions, is crucial for this differentiation [1, 2, 4, 5].
